articles.title: Samsung OLED, Neo QLED et Mini LED : Darty baisse les prix de trois téléviseurs, à partir de 569 euros
articles.text:
C’est la rentrée, vous voilà revenu dans votre canapé et vous ne pouvez pas vous empêcher de remarquer que votre téléviseur aurait bien besoin d’un coup de jeune. Darty profite de cette période charnière dans le renouvellement de son équipement pour faire baisser le prix de plusieurs téléviseurs Samsung.
La bonne nouvelle, c’est qu’il y en a pour tous les budgets. L’enseigne ne concentre pas ses remises sur les téléviseurs les plus premium, puisque des références OLED, Neo QLED, Mini LED et Micro RGB sont concernées par les offres.
- le téléviseur Samsung OLED TQ55S92H passe à 1 599 euros après une remise de 15 % ;
- le téléviseur Samsung Micro RGB TMR55R85H passe à 1 299 euros après une remise de 13 % ;
- le téléviseur Samsung Neo QLED TQ65QN74H passe à 899 euros après une remise de 10 % ;
- le téléviseur Samsung Mini LED TU55M80H passe à 569 euros après une remise de 9 %.
TV Samsung OLED TQ55S92H (55 pouces) à -15 %
L’OLED reste la technologie d’écran reine lorsqu’il s’agit de regarder du cinéma. Grâce à leurs pixels auto-émissifs, les écrans OLED proposent les meilleurs contrastes dans le monde des téléviseurs : les couleurs sont éclatantes tandis que les noirs sont très profonds.
Toutefois, l’OLED souffre d’un défaut : son pic lumineux en retrait et sa dalle brillante rendent son utilisation moins confortable en plein jour. Une faiblesse historique que Samsung vient corriger avec son téléviseur OLED TQ55S92H.
Le constructeur coréen l’a en effet équipé d’un filtre antireflet particulièrement performant. La texture de la dalle parvient à absorber la luminosité ambiante pour gommer les reflets. Plus besoin de se plonger dans le noir pour profiter de toutes les qualités de l’OLED.
Pour le reste de la fiche technique, Samsung fait peu de compromis : compatibilité HDR10+, dalle 165 Hz, présence de 4 ports HDMI 2.1 avec FreeSync Premium Pro et Nvidia G-Sync. Ajoutez l’interface Tizen et ses nombreuses applications et vous obtenez là le téléviseur idéal pour le cinéma, le divertissement et le jeu vidéo.
Pour la rentrée, Darty fait baisser le prix du téléviseur 55 pouces Samsung OLED TQ55S92H de 15 %, pour atteindre le prix final de 1 599 euros.
TV Samsung Micro RGB TMR55R85H (55 pouces) à -13 %
Avec l’OLED et le Mini LED, Samsung mise sur une nouvelle technologie pour ses téléviseurs haut de gamme : le Micro RGB. Son principe repose sur de minuscules LED rouges, vertes et bleues de moins de 100 micromètres, utilisées pour le rétroéclairage.
En contrôlant plus précisément chaque couleur dès la source lumineuse, cette technologie permet d’afficher une palette de couleurs particulièrement étendue. Samsung annonce ainsi une couverture de 100 % de l’espace colorimétrique BT.2020 sur son R85H. De quoi obtenir des couleurs plus riches et précises, tout en conservant une forte luminosité.
Le Samsung R85H profite également du Micro RGB AI Engine, chargé d’optimiser les couleurs, les contrastes et la définition de l’image. La compatibilité HDR10+ est aussi de la partie pour mieux restituer les détails dans les zones sombres comme lumineuses.
Pour le jeu vidéo, le téléviseur dispose d’une dalle 4K capable de monter jusqu’à 144 Hz en VRR. Ses quatre ports HDMI prennent en charge la 4K à 144 Hz, tandis que FreeSync Premium Pro vient compléter l’ensemble.
Enfin, Tizen se charge de toute la partie connectée, avec l’écosystème Samsung Vision AI et les nombreuses applications disponibles sur la plateforme.
Grâce à une remise de 13 %, le prix du téléviseur Samsung Micro RGB TMR55R85H passe à 1 299 euros dans sa version 55 pouces. D’autres diagonales sont par ailleurs en promotion.
TV Samsung Mini LED Neo QLED TQ65QN74H (65 pouces) à -10 %
Voilà quelques années maintenant qu’une nouvelle technologie est arrivée dans le monde des téléviseurs : le Mini LED. Cette évolution des téléviseurs LCD traditionnels utilise des LED plus petites, plus nombreuses, et donc avec une plus grande densité pour alimenter le rétroéclairage.
En résulte une image particulièrement lumineuse avec des contrastes pilotés plus précisément. Les meilleures télés Mini LED n’offrent pas encore la même profondeur des noirs que l’OLED, mais elles s’en rapprochent.
Avec son téléviseur Neo QLED TQ65QN74H, Samsung combine un rétroéclairage Mini LED avec un filtre Quantum Dots (QLED). Cette couche supplémentaire permet de mieux faire ressortir les couleurs, afin qu’elles soient plus riches et éclatantes. En associant le Mini LED et le Neo QLED, le téléviseur Samsung TQ65QN74H est capable d’afficher une image très lumineuse et flatteuse, que ce soit dans un environnement sombre ou éclairé.
Très à l’aise pour le cinéma avec sa compatibilité HDR10+, le téléviseur Samsung TQ65QN74H possède aussi de sérieux arguments pour le jeu vidéo. Il est compatible 120 Hz (en 2K), et profite de 3 ports HDMI 2.1 pour les consoles de nouvelle génération.
Encore une fois, Tizen est aux commandes de ce téléviseur pour lui apporter toute sa couche connectée : boutique d’applications et Samsung Vision AI sont de la partie.
Grâce à une remise de 10 % chez Darty, le téléviseur 65 pouces Samsung Mini LED Neo QLED TQ65QN74H passe à 899 euros.
TV Samsung Mini LED TU55M80H (55 pouces) à -9 %
Le Mini LED remplace progressivement les traditionnels LED, et c’est tant mieux pour le consommateur. Preuve en est sur le téléviseur de 55 pouces Samsung Mini LED TU55M80H affiché à 569 euros seulement.
Ce modèle petit budget hérite de la toute dernière technologie de rétroéclairage : le Mini LED. Certes, ces petites LED ne sont pas aussi nombreuses que sur les modèles plus haut de gamme, mais cela représente tout de même un sacré bond en avant face aux téléviseurs LED traditionnels.
Une meilleure finesse du rétroéclairage garantit une image plus contrastée et lumineuse, tout en parvenant à réduire l’effet « noir délavé ».
Malgré son prix, le téléviseur Samsung Mini LED TU55M80H affiche des caractéristiques particulièrement adaptées pour le jeu vidéo. Grâce à sa compatibilité 4K/144 Hz, la présence du VRR et de l’AMD FreeSync Premium, il exploite pleinement les caractéristiques des consoles de jeu de dernière génération, voire des PC de jeu.
Le TV Samsung Mini LED TU55M80H représente un achat malin compte tenu de son rapport qualité-prix et de la présence de Mini LED, d’autant plus lorsque son prix est en baisse chez Darty.

articles.title: Face à Starlink, Orange et Deutsche Telekom préparent un réseau satellitaire européen
articles.text:
Votre smartphone sait déjà appeler un satellite à la rescousse quand le réseau terrestre disparaît (du moins sur certains modèles, et pour de simples messages). Ce marché naissant, Starlink en a fait son terrain de jeu, au point d’inquiéter les opérateurs historiques du continent. Selon Bloomberg, Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone et Telefónica discuteraient ainsi d’une candidature commune sur une bande de fréquences stratégique, la 2 GHz, pour y bâtir un réseau satellitaire européen. Aucun des quatre n’a confirmé ces échanges pour le moment.
La bande 2 GHz, un vieux dossier que Bruxelles remet aux enchères
La bande en question réunit 30 MHz de fréquences pensées pour relier directement un satellite à un téléphone, sans antenne relais entre les deux. C’est le fameux « direct-to-device », dans le jargon du secteur : votre forfait continue de vivre là où aucun pylône ne pousse. L’Europe avait attribué ces fréquences en 2009 à Inmarsat (devenu Viasat entre-temps) et à Solaris (passé chez EchoStar). Les ambitions étaient grandes, le résultat est resté famélique : dix-sept ans plus tard, aucun service grand public d’envergure n’en est sorti. Un boulevard hertzien resté quasi désert, en somme.
Ces autorisations expirent en mai 2027, et la Commission a posé fin mai sa proposition de réattribution. Un tiers de la bande ira aux communications gouvernementales et militaires, adossé à la future constellation européenne IRIS². Le reste, dédié aux services commerciaux, sera coupé en deux : une moitié réservée à de nouveaux entrants européens, l’autre ouverte à tous les candidats. Les élus de la sélection paieront leur ticket d’entrée, redevances annuelles comprises, l’ouverture aux opérateurs virtuels étant par ailleurs encouragée. Ce découpage doit aussi nourrir le futur cadre européen des réseaux, le Digital Networks Act, que la Commission cite explicitement.
C’est la part réservée aux Européens que viseraient les quatre groupes, d’après les sources de Bloomberg. Une alliance n’a rien d’un réflexe naturel chez des maisons qui se disputent les mêmes clients depuis des décennies. Mais bâtir ou louer de la capacité satellitaire coûte une fortune, et aucun d’eux n’a la puissance de frappe de SpaceX. Une candidature groupée mutualise le risque, et la facture.
Starlink est déjà dans la place, et pas qu’un peu
Le calendrier de Bruxelles croise un autre dossier : SpaceX est en train de racheter une partie du spectre d’EchoStar, l’un des deux titulaires historiques de la bande. Sans garde-fou, des fréquences attribuées en 2009 à l’industrie satellitaire européenne pouvaient finir dans l’escarcelle d’Elon Musk. La Commission a donc verrouillé une partie du gâteau, et les opérateurs s’organisent pour la croquer.
Deutsche Telekom a déjà signé avec Starlink pour lancer le mobile par satellite en 2028 dans dix pays européens, Allemagne comprise, quand Vodafone partage à parts égales une coentreprise avec l’américain AST SpaceMobile. Le marché mondial de la connexion par satellite dépasse les 12 millions de connexions selon le cabinet CCS Insight, et l’essentiel vit chez Starlink. En clair, deux des quatre alliés potentiels ont déjà lié leur avenir satellitaire à des partenaires américains (un point de départ cocasse pour une reconquête européenne, on en conviendra).
Reste l’obstacle le plus européen qui soit : le calendrier législatif. Le Parlement et le Conseil doivent adopter le nouveau règlement avant mai 2027, faute de quoi les licences actuelles expireront sans régime de remplacement. Huit mois de navette pour un texte qui touche autant à la défense qu’au commerce : l’échéance est serrée.
Et pour votre forfait, ça change quoi ?
Le satellite dans le mobile n’est déjà plus une promesse lointaine. Apple propose ses SOS d’urgence par satellite sur iPhone depuis plusieurs années, et Orange vend depuis décembre 2025 son option Satellite Message construite avec l’opérateur Skylo sur des satellites géostationnaires de Viasat, ainsi qu’une offre internet avec Nordnet. Le service couvre l’envoi de messages dans plus de 30 pays européens, offert six mois aux abonnés 5G+ puis facturé 5 euros par mois, en attendant une extension aux appels vocaux. Malgré des années de résorption des zones blanches, la couverture mobile française garde ses trous : c’est précisément ce marché de la rustine que le satellite vient combler.
La bataille du 2 GHz décidera qui possédera l’étage au-dessus. Non plus un bouton d’urgence ou une option à quelques euros, mais une couverture de secours intégrée au forfait, pour les messages, la voix et les données. La Commission cite d’ailleurs la liaison directe aux smartphones et l’Internet des objets parmi les usages attendus de la bande : les randonneurs ne seront pas les seuls servis, vos capteurs isolés aussi. Si les quatre opérateurs vont au bout, cette couverture serait européenne de bout en bout, fréquences comprises. Le calendrier, lui, reste entièrement à écrire : il faudra un règlement voté, des satellites en orbite, des accords entre les quatre maisons et des téléphones compatibles (rien d’insurmontable, rien d’immédiat non plus).

articles.text:
Howdy. ☀️️

Banking
Portuguese lender is leaving Angola after 30 years and selling its stake for $451 million
For a bank, leaving a country isn’t as simple as switching off an app and sending everyone a breakup email—or treating it like some rapture. 👀 Market exits, for banks, are more measured. Banco BPI, a Portuguese commercial bank, has spent almost a decade trying to leave Angola. Now, after 30 years in the country, it seems it is finally time to hand over the keys.
What happened? On September 3, Portuguese lender Banco BPI agreed to sell its remaining 33.35% stake in Banco de Fomento Angola (BFA) to Congolian Financial SA (CFSA), a company owned by Angolan conglomerate Grupo Carrinho, for nearly $451 million. The deal still needs approval from Angola’s Central Bank and Capital Markets Commission. If it gets the green light, BPI will have sold its entire interest in BFA and officially ended its three-decade run in Angola.
Explain like I’m new here: BPI entered the country in 1996, when it acquired the Angolan operations of Portuguese lender Banco de Fomento e Exterior and eventually turned them into BFA. BFA became a separately incorporated Angolan bank in July 2002, initially 100% controlled by BPI. Then, in 2008, BPI sold 49.9% of BFA to Unitel, Angola’s biggest telecom operator. In 2017, it sold another 2% to Unitel, giving up control of the bank to CaixaBank.
BPI really wanted out: BPI’s efforts to reduce its Angola exposure predated the ECB’s 2017 pressure. In 2015, the bank said it planned to spin off its African assets into a separate entity to limit its exposure to risks in Angola. This came after European Union (EU) rules classified Angolan credit and debt exposure as risky assets that had to be fully provisioned for under European rules.
In 2017, the European Central Bank (ECB) then pushed BPI to further reduce its Angola exposure, citing concerns around Angola’s banking supervision and capital requirements. BPI spent years looking for investors to buy its remaining 48.1% stake.
Grupo Carrinho was among the potential buyers; however, in 2023, a sharp depreciation of the Angolan Kwanza against the US Dollar complicated negotiations. BPI eventually suspended the sale. In 2025, it found another way to shrink its position by listing on Angola’s stock exchange. BPI sold 14.75% of the bank through the listing, cutting its stake to the 33.35% it is now selling.
Who gets the keys? Grupo Carrinho started as a small catering business in 1993 and grew into one of Angola’s biggest agro-industrial groups. It is also becoming a serious player in banking. Carrinho already owns 74% of Banco de Comércio e Indústria (BCI) and about 70% of Banco Keve. This story is one of a local conglomerate getting a much bigger seat at one of the country’s biggest banks.
Every business owner needs to watch this.
The business questions you Google, answered by experts. Watch for free .
Streaming
DStv is reshuffling its channels and packages; what changes for you?
If you’ve ever paid more for DStv because the channel you really wanted was trapped in a pricier package (side-eye MultiChoice and its expensive English Premier League access package), DStv is about to make things a little less rigid… at least we hope.
What happened? MultiChoice, Africa’s largest pay-TV operator, is changing its package lineup. From September 17, DStv is discontinuing the Compact Plus tier; sports gets its own package, and some channels that were previously locked inside Premium are becoming available in cheaper packages. Starter, Select, and Sports packages will replace the current Access, Family, and Compact packages, while a new Movies & Series package will also join the lineup.
Explain like I’m new here: In August, MultiChoice announced it would shut down four DStv channels (M-Net Movies 1, Mzansi Bioskop, Mzansi Music, and KykNet Lekker) on September 16. It replaced them with four new SuperSport channels focused on premium football and major African sporting events. Showmax has since been discontinued, while DStv Stream took centre stage; it also discontinued entertainment channels BET Africa and MTV Base in January. This is all part of a reshuffle under French owner Canal+.
What changes for you: If you’re on Access, you’ll move to Starter for R150 ($9.40) monthly on satellite. Family becomes Select at R339 (21.25). If you’re on Compact, you’ll move to Sports for R479 ($30.03) on satellite or R399 ($25.02) on DStv Stream. You’ll also get 17 sports channels, including every Premier League and Champions League match, plus all cricket and major local rugby competitions. If you’re on Compact Plus, you’ll be moved to Premium because Compact Plus is being discontinued. You’ll keep paying your current price for 12 months. After that, you’ll need to decide whether to pay the new Premium price or switch to another package.
Why is DStv doing this? DStv has seen that subscribers are downgrading when they can no longer justify expensive packages. Instead of making customers choose between paying for channels they don’t watch or cancelling altogether, MultiChoice is making its packages more modular. Sports fans can pay for Sports without buying the full Premium bundle, while movie and entertainment fans can subscribe to Movies & Series. Cheaper, tailored packages give customers a reason to stay.
Moonshot is back!
Moonshot 2026 is coming! Join us at the National Theatre, Lagos on October 28 & 29 for two days of tech and innovation. Grab your early bird tickets now and get 15% off .
Government
Ghana launches digital marriage records platform
In our newsroom, we always say, “there’s tech in everything.” We should probably update that thesis to “there’s an AI use case for everything; you just haven’t figured it out.” An African government using tech and AI for marriage records wasn’t on our bingo card for 2026, but bet against Ghana at your own detriment.
What happened? Ghana has launched Marrify, a digital platform that lets people search and verify registered marriage and divorce records. It can also verify marriage officers, licensed venues, churches, pastors, and imams, while an AI assistant provides contextual information on Ghanaian marriage law.
Why it matters: If, at work, you become suspicious of your colleague who has a secret family but keeps denying that they are married, Marrify is your friend in Ghana. (wink)
More seriously, Marrify turns marriage records from something people largely have to chase through offices and institutions into searchable digital infrastructure. That has obvious value when you need to verify whether a prospective spouse has a registered marriage or divorce. Still, it also matters for inheritance, immigration, property disputes, court cases, and other situations where knowing someone’s legal marital status can have consequences. The same goes for checking whether a pastor, imam, marriage officer, or venue is actually authorised to conduct marriages.
But there’s a drawback: Marriage and divorce records are sensitive personal information. Making them easier to access can reduce fraud and bureaucracy, but it can also make stalking, harassment, unwanted disclosure, and other forms of misuse easier if the safeguards are weak.
The bigger picture: The opportunity is what happens when all that information is brought together. Marrify says it pulls data from the Registrar-General’s Department, courts, local assemblies, and the Ghana Gazette. For citizens, that could mean less running around government offices for basic verification. For courts and government agencies, it could mean faster document checks and fewer opportunities for people to exploit gaps between different records.
Yet, Marrify cannot be a magic marital-status truth machine. Ghana recognises ordinance, customary and Islamic marriages, and they do not all follow the same registration process. A person not appearing in the database could mean they were never married. Still, it could also mean their marriage was registered elsewhere, the record has not been digitised or linked yet, or the information entered does not match what is in the registry.
Zoom out: Ghana is showing what digital government can look like when it tackles very ordinary problems. The interesting part isn’t even the AI or tech; it’s whether the country can build enough trust in the underlying data for people to use the platform credibly, and how much more of its public records it can digitise.
Fintech
Mukuru wants Botswana’s phones to do more than receive money
Botswana has more mobile connections than people, but a surprising number of those people still don’t have a bank account. In 2025, there were about 4.22 million active mobile connections, nearly twice as many as the country’s 2.56 million people; about 650,000 of the country’s adult population are unbanked.
People have phones; many just aren’t using traditional bank accounts. Mukuru sees an opportunity in that mismatch.
What happened? The remittance company launched its Companion Card in Botswana in August, giving customers a Visa card linked directly to their Mukuru Wallet. Money can move from the wallet to the supermarket, taxi, electricity bill, or online checkout without first passing through a bank account or cash point.
Explain like I’m new here: Someone receives money in their Mukuru Wallet. Instead of withdrawing it as cash before spending it, they can now pay directly from the wallet wherever Visa is accepted.
State of play: Mukuru is betting that financial inclusion doesn’t have to begin with a bank. Customers already using its wallet can now do more with it without changing how they receive money. Banks still have the edge in savings, credit, and other financial products. Wallets can compete on access and simplicity. Mukuru is trying to close some of that gap.
Zoom out: The bigger opportunity is customer behaviour. A company that simply helps you receive money only processes a transaction. A company whose wallet you use to pay for groceries, transport, and bills will build a deeper relationship.
If Mukuru can make its wallet part of everyday spending, the Companion Card becomes more than a convenient way to spend remittances. It becomes a way to turn a remittance product into a genuine alternative to a bank account.

articles.title: México afronta un nuevo reto en la reducción de la jornada a 40 horas: que los empleados puedan comer
articles.text:
Falta poco más de un año para que la semana laboral en México empiece a reducirse de las 48 horas actuales a las 40 horas semanales que deben alcanzar en 2030. Es ahora cuando empresas y trabajadores deben afrontar el reto de organizar el trabajo para continuar produciendo lo mismo, pero aprovechando mejor el tiempo de la jornada laboral.
Uno de los escollos que están encontrando los empleadores en esa búsqueda choca frontalmente con la normativa aprobada a principios de año por el Senado. Está en juego quién decide si comes, o si trabajas, esos los 30 minutos para comer que la Ley Federal del Trabajo garantiza a todos los empleados.
Se ha iniciado la cuenta atrás. La reforma que reduce la jornada de 48 a 40 horas entró en vigor el 1 de mayo de 2026, coincidiendo con el Día Internacional de los Trabajadores. El cambio de jornada laboral será progresivo, pero el reloj ya ha comenzado a correr y la primera rebaja de jornada llegará el 1 de enero de 2027, cuando el máximo baje de 48 horas a 46 horas semanales.
Desde ahí, el recorte sigue a razón de dos horas cada año hasta terminar en las 40 horas semanales en 2030. Con ese paso, México se coloca entre los tres países con la jornada más corta de Latinoamérica. Solo por detrás de Ecuador y Chile.
La comida, un derecho que la ley blinda. No obstante, la reducción de la jornada no puede traducirse como una merma salarial o de derechos laborales de los trabajadores, sino que se busca una optimización del tiempo que los empleados pasan en sus puestos de trabajo.
En este punto, las empresas se han encontrado con un escollo blindado por el artículo 63 de la Ley Federal del Trabajo que establece que durante la jornada continua, "se concederá al trabajador un descanso de media hora, por lo menos". Además, el artículo 64 de la Ley Federal del Trabajo indica que si el trabajador no puede salir del centro de trabajo en ese tiempo de descanso, la ley va más allá y establece que ese tiempo computa como jornada laboral y, como tal, hay que pagarlo como tiempo de trabajo ya que el empleado permanece a disposición del patrón.
Así lo establecen varias tesis de La Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación (equivalente al Tribunal Supremo en España). La única excepción que contempla el Alto Tribunal es que se produzca en un contexto de jornada a tiempo parcial inferior a las ocho horas de la jornada completa, en cuyo caso deja de ser a obligatorio y se deja en manos de una revisión que tenga en cuenta la naturaleza del trabajo.
Por qué las empresas quieren tocarla. Las distintas plataformas patronales han venido exponiendo sus preocupaciones y argumentos en los diferentes foros que la Secretaría del Trabajo y Previsión Social organizó entre 2025 y 2026, cuando se aprobó el texto definitivo.
Si la jornada laboral se acorta, hay que aprovechar cada minuto que el empleado pasa en el puesto de trabajo. Por eso, algunos patrones plantean borrar los llamados "tiempos muertos" y, entre ellos, la pausa de 30 minutos obligatoria. La idea es que trabajar ocho horas seguidas, sin interrupciones, compensaría el día libre extra que recoge la reforma laboral.
El gobierno cierra la puerta, por ahora. El titular de la Secretaría del Trabajo, Marath Bolaños, salió al paso y ha insistido en que la transición a 40 horas no borra ningún derecho ya ganado, como así lo detalla la propia normativa.
El mensaje oficial deja poco margen para interpretaciones libres y, con la actual formulación de los artículos 63 y 64 de la ley, las empresas deberán asumir la optimización de la jornada sin tocar el derecho al descanso de los empleados y, si se destina a ese fin, respetar su tiempo para comer. Alterar esa condición supondría abordar otra reforma de esos artículos.
La realidad ya va por otro camino. Mientras se discute la letra pequeña, los datos pintan un país que ya trabaja más horas de las que dictan sus leyes, según revela el último boletín de la Encuesta Nacional de Ocupación y Empleo del INEGI. De acuerdo a estos datos, 9,2 millones de personas aseguraron trabajar jornadas de más de 48 horas semanales en el segundo trimestre de 2026.
Aunque la reforma ya esté en marcha, esta cifra sigue subiendo. La ley puede fijar límites nuevos, claros y por escrito. Pero su fuerza real depende de vigilancia en la aplicación de la reducción de la jornada laboral con ajuste a la ley, y de que ningún empleador confunda "optimizar la jornada" con reducir los derechos de los trabajadores.

articles.title: Old School RuneScape developer sentenced for stealing and selling in-game virtual gold
articles.text:
Retro-Thief: A RuneScape developer tried to make a quick buck out of the online RPG. The company eventually discovered the internal culprit after setting a trap, and the hacker has now been sentenced while detectives are still trying to recover the money he stole.
Stealing virtual gold coins can earn some real-world money, even in retro-focused experiences such as Old School RuneScape. A developer named Andrew Lakeman tried to abuse his privileged position as a content creator working at Jagex, but a years-long investigation has illustrated that crime does not pay – no matter how retro your MMORPG target is.
The investigation was led by Andrew McKeane, a detective working with the Cambridgeshire Constabulary. Lakeman began working at RuneScape studio Jagex in November 2015, but his plan was set in motion a few years later. In 2018, Jagex's support team noticed suspicious activity related to several account recovery instances.
The accounts in question had been stripped of their in-game items, including virtual coins. Jagex eventually confirmed that someone within the company was stealing the virtual goods, so it opened an internal investigation and set a trap to identify the hacker. The plan worked, and the British studio was able to trace the illicit activity back to Lakeman's home address and devices.
The developer first claimed that his own account had been hacked, but he was ultimately fired. At the same time, Jagex passed the investigation to Cambridgeshire police in 2019. The law enforcement agency eventually discovered that Lakeman was planning to make a small fortune by selling in-game content on the black market. The hacker had already amassed £364,829 ($493,000) in cryptocurrencies, including £300,000 from his internal theft at Old School RuneScape.
Cambridgeshire's investigation came to an end earlier this month. Lakeman pleaded guilty to his virtual-yet-very-real crimes, but had his three-year sentence suspended for two years by the Cambridge Crown Court. Furthermore, the court decided that the hacker must carry out 150 hours of unpaid community work, as well as a 25-day rehabilitation period. The investigators are now trying to recover the money Lakeman earned through his crypto transactions.
Detective Constable McKeane highlighted how sentencing Lakeman required an unusually complex investigation. The hacker knew rather well that what he was doing was a crime, and virtual crimes are still subject to real-world laws.
"Given the rapid growth of online and virtual worlds, the justice system is going to have to keep pace and adapt to these new and emerging crimes," the court said.
Old School RuneScape is a free fantasy MMORPG based on a 2007 backup Jagex discovered in its archives. The British studio eventually launched a "modern" rendition of RuneScape in 2020, with both versions now being maintained by their corresponding communities. Despite being a free-to-play experience, the whole RuneScape experience has so far generated $3 billion in revenue.

articles.title: Nintendo’s Ocarina of Time remake launches in November
articles.text:
Link’s next adventure now has a release date. During a Legend of Zelda stream for the franchise’s 40th anniversary, Nintendo announced that the upcoming Ocarina of Time remake for the Switch 2 is launching on November 5th. The release date makes Ocarina of Time one of just a few big-budget titles launching in the same month as Grand Theft Auto VI.
Nintendo’s Ocarina of Time remake launches in November
The company showed off its next Switch 2 showcase during a Zelda anniversary stream.
Nintendo first teased the remake in June, though it didn’t reveal much aside from a brief trailer. Today’s event provided a clearer glimpse at how the company is approaching remaking one of its most influential games and the first 3D Zelda adventure. The updated version of Ocarina of Time will be the first Zelda release that’s exclusive to the Switch 2, and longtime Zelda producer Eiji Aonuma described the remake as “a faithful interpretation using modern technologies.”
The gameplay shown at the event revealed much more detailed graphics compared to the N64 original — including an intimidating take on the Great Deku Tree and a surprisingly fancy hat for Link — along with free camera movement. Other new features include something called “threads of time,” which makes it easier to see where (and when) your next destination is, and the ability to hum tunes in the game instead of playing them via the controller. Also: Link can jump now when you press a button. You can watch the demonstration below:
A digital copy of Ocarina of Time will cost $59.99, while a physical copy will cost $69.99.
In other Zelda news, Nintendo also confirmed that the upcoming live-action movie will be titled simply The Legend of Zelda. It hits theaters on April 30th, 2027.
While today’s event featured a bunch of Zelda updates, there’s still more on the way from Nintendo: The company is holding a second Direct stream on September 9th at 10AM ET, which will be 45 minutes long and focus on Switch 2 games launching later in 2026.
Update, September 8th: Added prices.

articles.title: This geneticist’s age-reversal tech could help restore sight
articles.text:
This geneticist’s age-reversal tech could help restore sight
Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu is behind one of the buzziest results in rejuvenation science.
Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu is obsessed with aging. And with eyes. As he steps outside the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts, his aviator glasses darken automatically in the sun. Age-related blindness runs in his family. A great-aunt in China, the story goes, was killed crossing a road because she couldn’t see oncoming traffic. And Lu’s own 23andMe test came back with a mutation for macular degeneration, a top cause of vision loss in old age. Exposure to bright sunlight is another risk factor—thus the shades. “They protect me,” he says. “Plus, they look cool.”
Lu, 34, works on gene therapies to prevent age-related vision loss. “I think the eye is a really unique system to study aging and rejuvenation,” he says. “I could give a whole presentation.” Pushing up my reading glasses, I lean in to listen.
Lu is behind one of the coolest results in rejuvenation science—and in eye research. In 2018, while earning his PhD at Harvard Medical School, he used an age-reversal technique called reprogramming to repair the optic nerves of mice. He crushed the nerves, blinding the animals, and then injected the cells with a gene therapy meant to restore them to a youthful state. Sixteen days later, the nerves were growing back, their axons showing up through a microscope as spidery orange filaments.
 As hype around age reversal swirls, Lu has been busy in the lab searching for what he calls “the next generation of rejuvenation therapies.”
The head of that lab, the longevity scientist David Sinclair, remembers when Lu texted him the pictures: “He asked me, ‘What do you see here?’ And I said, ‘I see the future.’” Later tests carried out in a box with rotating bars of light showed the mice were tracking the changes. They could see again.
This year, nearly the exact genetic therapy Lu created for mice entered human clinical trials. On June 9, the startup Life Biosciences, which Sinclair cofounded and in which Lu owns a small stake, announced it had injected the treatment into the eye of a person with glaucoma. The trial has been big news. A headline in the New York Times suggested the technology could “change humanity.” Posters on X gushed, with one declaring that “the fountain of youth is here.”
“It’s remarkable that what he developed as a student is now going into humans,” says Sinclair of the treatment, now called ER-100. “It’s barely even changed since he built it.”
Reprogramming refers to an age-restoring process that takes place inside an embryo. It’s why babies are born young, not old: The DNA they’ve inherited from their parents has been scrubbed and reset. In 2006, Japanese researchers showed they could cause the process to occur in the lab by introducing just four key genes, known by the acronym OSKM. Add these to a cell from a 100-year-old and it will turn into a stem cell that acts as if it was plucked from an embryo.
That’s powerful stuff. But we don’t want to turn people into blobs of stem-cell protoplasm. Lu figured out a way to control the effect. He trimmed the list of genes to just OSK—leaving out M, for Myc, the one most likely to cause dangerous changes like cancer. His extra flash of insight was that reprogramming could be tested on the optic nerve; the eye is particularly accessible.
Lu’s result, published in Nature in 2020, helped set off an investment rush. Since then, US tech billionaires have placed huge bets on private companies like Altos Labs and NewLimit to explore reprogramming and anti-aging medicine. The day I spoke with Lu, he’d spent the morning meeting with the business magnate Zhong Shanshan, one of China’s richest people.
Still, as hype around age reversal swirls, Lu has been notably absent from the public conversation. He’s been busy in the lab searching for what he calls “the next generation of rejuvenation therapies.” With a sigh, Lu describes the grueling effort over the last six years to understand what OSK really does. The treatment remains toxic to many cell types, and he says it’s becoming obvious that different factors drive aging in each kind. This year, for example, he identified a gene responsible for protecting the retina from damage by free radicals—the main cause of age-related macular degeneration.
While Sinclair, his former boss, believes humans could live to be 200, Lu disagrees. There’s just too much that goes wrong as we age. His work with OSK, he says, was more a proof of concept than a silver bullet. But it did change the conversation. “Six years ago, you couldn’t talk about rejuvenation. We didn’t use that word—there was pushback,” Lu tells me. “But I think people have accepted the concept that you can really reverse molecular age.”
Deep Dive
Biotechnology and health
Sperm donors need limits, says a European fertility group
Some donor-conceived people are finding hundreds of siblings. An international cap on donations could help prevent that.
A startup claims it’s found a drug to make your blood young
Generation Lab claims its drug combo can “stop the spread of aging” around the body. And it’s looking for influencers to give it a try.
Montana’s plan to become an experimental medical hub just pushed forward
The state’s effort to expand the “right to try” is making headway, and the first drugs are about to be reviewed.
There’s a lot of hype around perimenopause. Don’t buy it.
Discussions of the life stage are often clouded by misinformation.

articles.title: Almost all AI tools are now running with no oversight from IT — putting companies in the firing line
articles.text:
Almost all AI tools are now running with no oversight from IT — putting companies in the firing line
Someone hasn’t locked the door
- Report claims an incredible 80% of AI tools are running in organizations without IT oversight
- Browser agents and integration tools are escaping the attention of security and IT engineers
- Reco’s State of Agent Security 2026 report also tracked 637 vulnerabilities across agents and LLMs
Unmonitored deployment of AI tools is a risk to security, and puts data at risk, a new study has claimed.
The report from Reco, which draws its information from disclosed vulnerabilities, analysis of 500 Model Context Protocol servers, and Reco’s own platform telemetry, found four in five AI tools (80%) are running without oversight from IT departments.
Of particular concern is the scale of AI applications in use. Smaller companies use 414 AI tools per 1,000 employees without IT approval, apparently a combination of browser extensions and workflows beyond the usual review and approval process.
Data risks from unmonitored AI
Giving AI tools to employees might unlock productivity boosts, but their use has to be approved. That’s the key takeaway from the report, which highlights some concerning cybersecurity figures. For example, it assessed 500 agent tools and found “62% can both read local data and reach the internet.” This represents an opportunity for data exfiltration.
Elsewhere, 637 AI agent related vulnerabilities were identified in the report.
The adoption of AI is wider than specific use of a SaaS application or visiting ChatGPT. Reco found that AI agents are running within other tools, and inheriting user permissions. The implications of this are clear.
Operational risk
Analysis of the telemetry (gathered from 62 enterprise-scale businesses in financial services, healthcare, retail, and telecommunications between January 1 and August 1 2026) reveals a free-for-all attitude towards AI adoption. While businesses may have policies and procedures in place and processes to assess, evaluate, review, and finally approve new AI-based tools, these are being circumvented for low-level applications.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The rules work for SaaS procurement oversight, but not for browser extensions, and the result is “operational risk.”
“AI agents have moved from experimentation into daily business workflows, but our findings show only 20% of AI tools in enterprise ecosystems are currently governed by IT oversight," Reco CEO Ofer Klein noted.
“That leaves organizations exposed to a new class of operational risk. Agents embedded in applications can operate through existing permissions, OAuth grants and workflow access, creating toxic combinations that expose data and trigger actions beyond what any owner approved.”
Organizations will need to give IT teams the resources they need to manage and restrict unauthorized AI use, as the alternative means leaving the gates open to the possibility of data exfiltration.

Christian Cawley has extensive experience as a writer and editor in consumer electronics, IT and entertainment media. He has contributed to TechRadar since 2017 and has been published in Computer Weekly, Linux Format, ComputerActive, and other publications.
He currently heads up the team at smart home website Matter Alpha, and writes about retro gaming at Gaming Retro.

articles.title: La nueva función de WhatsApp te permitirá chatear y controlar agentes de IA dentro de la app
articles.text:
WhatsApp prepara una nueva función que te permitirá chatear con varios agentes de IA. La compañía lanzó una actualización con chats dedicados para agentes de terceros para hablar con ellos en una conversación por separado. Si bien el cliente de mensajería ya cuenta con una IA que puede ejecutar múltiples acciones, todavía no es posible integrar otros modelos que no pertenezcan a Meta a la plataforma.
La nueva función, reportada por WABetaInfo, aparece en la actualización más reciente de la beta para Android. Una vez que la instalas, aparecerá una opción dentro de los ajustes de la app que te permite conectar a un agente externo y hablar con él. La configuración es relativamente sencilla y solo requiere conectarla a través de una API con el servicio en donde vive tu IA.
En términos de funcionamiento, WhatsApp permite vincular hasta cinco agentes distintos por cuenta, cada uno con nombre y foto de perfil asignados que lucirán como cualquier otro contacto en tu lista de chats. Los usuarios pueden hacer preguntas en la ventana de conversación o darle instrucciones para que lleve a cabo tareas en tu nombre. Si alguna vez usaste OpenClaw, entonces sabrás lo que puedes hacer cuando tienes a varios agentes bajo tu mando.
Antes de emocionarse y pensar en crear un grupo con todos ellos, hay algunos detalles a considerar. El primero y más importante es que la función solo es compatible con chats individuales, así que olvídate de añadirlo a tu grupo de amigos o a alguna comunidad. El agente solo puede leer lo que le compartes en la ventana de conversación, por lo que no tendrá acceso a tus contactos ni tus archivos multimedia.
WhatsApp te permitirá configurar hasta cinco agentes por cuenta
Sobre esta línea, si usas un agente deberás ser consciente de que las conversaciones no están cifradas de extremo a extremo. A diferencia de los chats habituales, WhatsApp no puede blindar lo que le dices al agente para que nadie lo lea durante el proceso. Esto se debe a que los chats con los agentes pasan por un servicio de Meta que actúa en representación del desarrollador externo, el cual puede acceder a esos mensajes como parte del funcionamiento del servicio.
WhatsApp ofrece una gestión básica sobre los agentes una vez que ya los creaste. Si quieres cambiar el nombre o la foto de perfil, solo tienes que acceder a la configuración para ajustar los valores. También es posible eliminarlo, aunque esta acción es irreversible y ya no podrás conversar con él. La buena noticia es que el historial y la ventana de chat se almacenan en el historial para que accedas a ellos cuando quieras.
Los agentes de terceros están disponible en la versión 2.26.35.3 de la beta de WhatsApp para Android. El reporte menciona que el despliegue es gradual, por lo que no todos los usuarios que participan en el programa podrán acceder a él. Por el momento no hay detalles sobre un despliegue más amplio, aunque tratándose de IA, es probable que ocurra pronto.

articles.title: Renault, Stellantis et Aramis Auto s'engagent à afficher la santé des batteries d'occasion
articles.text:
Monique Barbut, ministre de la Transition écologique, a réuni la filière automobile le vendredi 4 septembre à Rambouillet, dans une concession Peugeot. Dans une publication sur LinkedIn, on apprend ainsi que Renault, Stellantis et le spécialiste de l’occasion Aramis Auto y ont signé un « pacte de confiance ». Les trois acteurs se sont engagés à afficher le SoH (State of Health), le pourcentage de capacité qu’il reste à la batterie par rapport au neuf, des voitures électriques d’occasion vendues dans leur réseau de concessions.
Au-delà des trois acteurs, le pacte a également été signé par les organisations du secteur, dont Mobilians, la Plateforme automobile (PFA) et la CSIAM, qui représentent constructeurs et distributeurs.
L’électrique d’occasion désormais soutenue par l’État
Le calendrier n’a rien d’un hasard. Une série d’aides à l’achat pour les voitures électriques d’occasion est entrée en vigueur le 1er septembre. La principale, adossée aux certificats d’économies d’énergie (CEE) et financée par les fournisseurs d’énergie, monte jusqu’à 400 € pour un modèle 100 % électrique immatriculé entre 2017 et 2023. Ce montant peut grimper entre 2 000 et 2 360 € jusqu’à la fin de l’année 2026 pour les professionnels de l’aide à domicile et des services à la personne.
Si l’aide n’impose aucune condition de revenus pour y prétendre, elle fait entrer d’autres critères en jeu pour la voiture :
- 80 % de capacité restante (SoH) minimum ou à défaut autonomie résiduelle supérieure à 200 km ou 80 % de l’autonomie WLTP
- Moins de 25 000 €
- Moins de 1 800 kg
- être achetée ou louée chez un professionnel
- être conservée au moins 3 ans (ou louée minimum 3 ans)
Une donnée que le vendeur ne maîtrise pas toujours
Sur le papier, l’engagement paraît modeste, puisqu’une partie des professionnels affichait déjà cette valeur, tandis qu’Aramis certifie l’état de santé de ses batteries depuis 2020. D’autant plus que le pacte reste un engagement volontaire, sans sanction pour les concessions qui l’ignoreraient. Certains pointent aussi du doigt le fait que cette certification du SoH ne vient pas d’un organisme indépendant.
La mesure a malgré tout de quoi rassurer l’acheteur potentiel. L’état de la batterie est « généralement l’élément le plus freinant dans l’acquisition d’un véhicule électrique d’occasion », a souligné la ministre.
La mesure française devance une future obligation européenne. À partir du 18 février 2027, l’Union européenne imposera progressivement un « passeport batterie », consultable via un QR code.

articles.title: Sony ressort l'un de ses meilleurs casques, avec une surprise sur le prix
articles.text:
Face à un WH-1000XM6 affiché à 449 euros (mais que l’on retrouve déjà bien moins cher), le constructeur japonais tente d’occuper le terrain du haut de gamme plus abordable avec son nouveau casque audio, le Sony WH-1000XM4C. Au lieu de concevoir une référence inédite, la marque pioche dans son historique et réintroduit son ancien champion de 2020, le WH-1000XM4. Une stratégie qui n’est pas sans rappeler celle de Bose avec ses QC Headphones.
L’ancien roi des casques Bluetooth fait son come-back
Niveau design, Sony conserve la structure circum-auriculaire d’origine. Le WH-1000XM4C garde ses lignes rétro, son format repliable bien plus pratique pour le transport que certaines générations intermédiaires comme le WH-1000XM5, et sa connectique complète. La prise jack 3,5 mm répond toujours présente, y compris pour une écoute passive casque éteint. Seul un nouveau coloris Lavande vient signaler le changement de cuvée aux côtés des versions Noir et Platinum Silver. Côté connectivité, l’appareil intègre une puce Bluetooth 6.0 et supporte la fonction Fast Pair sur Android, mais le LE Audio et l’USB audio manquent à l’appel.
Sous l’arceau, l’architecture interne reste quasi identique au modèle de 2020. On retrouve le transducteur de 40 mm épaulé par la puce de traitement QN1 et un ensemble de microphones dédiés à la réduction de bruit active. La nouveauté vient de l’audio : Sony applique sa « dernière signature sonore », identique à celle du XM6, combinée à un égaliseur 10 bandes géré dans l’application Sound Connect. L’autonomie atteint 20 heures avec la réduction de bruit active et monte à 27 heures sans. Positionné à 249,99 euros, le casque vise clairement ceux qui hésitent à dépenser plus de 400 euros dans le dernier modèle haut de gamme de la marque.
Deux autres casques sans-fil pas chers
Pour compléter son catalogue, Sony rafraîchit son entrée de gamme avec les WH-CH730N et WH-CH530, déclinés en six coloris. Affiché à 120 euros, le CH730N mise sur un format circum-auriculaire léger de 207 grammes à structure pliable. Équipé d’un haut-parleur de 30 mm, il prend en charge le LE Audio, l’Auracast, ainsi que la technologie d’amélioration sonore DSEE. Sa réduction de bruit s’ajuste sur 20 niveaux et son autonomie grimpe jusqu’à 50 heures avec réduction de bruit, ou 75 heures sans. Il ajoute un préréglage Game EQ conçu avec la branche Inzone.
Beaucoup plus basique, le WH-CH530 ferme la marche pour seulement 59 euros. Ce modèle adopte une conception supra-auriculaire où les coussinets reposent directement sur les oreilles, sans proposer d’isolation active. Il reprend l’essentiel des fonctions et réglages sonores de son grand frère, se concentrant sur la simplicité d’utilisation. Ces deux références plus accessibles partagent avec le XM4c le support de Fast Pair sur Android et une disponibilité calée sur ce mois de septembre.

articles.title: Smart vs. Dumb Security & Surveillance: Why the Best Systems Use a Bit of Both - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Imagine your business spending a small fortune installing a cutting-edge surveillance system, one where the cameras can recognise faces, distinguish people from vehicles and send an alert the instant something suspicious happens.
And then imagine one camera pointed slightly too high. For the next six months, the world’s most sophisticated security system becomes exceptionally good at monitoring a roof.
It might be somewhat of a silly example, but it makes an important point that better technology doesn’t automatically mean better security. A smart system still depends on the basics being right. The best security setups combine intelligent technology with simpler, proven measures because sometimes a strong lock, bright light or visible camera is exactly what a property needs.
Why Security Works Best as a Layered Approach
Commercial security relies on you creating layers that make unwanted access harder, detect suspicious behaviour and ensure someone can respond when something happens. A business might combine physical barriers, conventional CCTV, access control, alarms, lighting and security personnel with intelligent monitoring technologies.
For example, businesses considering more traditional, foolproof protection like mobile patrol security in Melbourne can combine physical patrols with smart surveillance. Cameras can identify unusual activity and alert a monitoring team, while patrol officers provide the physical presence needed to investigate or respond.
Something not separate, but combined like this, is ideal because every security technology has limitations. A camera can record an intruder, but it can’t physically stop them. An alarm can detect movement, but it doesn’t necessarily understand whether that movement represents a genuine threat. Layering these measures means one system can compensate when another reaches its limits.
What Makes Security ‘Smart’?
Smart security generally refers to systems capable of processing information, making automated decisions or communicating with other devices. Surveillance cameras that we find today are a good example. Intelligent cameras can analyse what they see, rather than just recording. Depending on the system, they may distinguish between people, vehicles and other movements, helping reduce unnecessary alerts.
Connected systems can go a step further. Let’s say a camera detects someone entering a restricted area, it can then trigger an alarm, notify a monitoring centre and provide a live video feed for verification. Access control systems can then record who enters a building and when, while connected alarms can flag unusual activity. The major advantage is efficiency, and efficiency in security is key to preventing crimes.
The Very Real Purpose of Dumb Security
‘Dumb security’ is definitely not foolish. Dumb security refers to security that doesn’t necessarily have advanced tech installed, like guards, alarms and fences. A security fence doesn’t need artificial intelligence, a sturdy lock doesn’t require an internet connection and a bright exterior light doesn’t need facial recognition. These tried-and-tested measures work because they address some of the oldest principles in security: deter, delay and detect.
Visible cameras are a very effective deterrent, putting off opportunistic offenders before an incident occurs. Simple security is also very reliable because it’s not relying on electronics, signals or software updates. As security systems are expected to work when something goes wrong, this leaves smart systems more vulnerable, as during a threat is precisely when technology can sometimes be under the greatest strain.
Where Smart Systems Really Shine
Smart technology becomes especially useful when businesses need to monitor large or complicated sites. Consider a warehouse with multiple entrances, loading areas, storage zones and vehicle access points. Watching every part of the property manually would be difficult and inefficient. Smart warehouse technology with intelligent surveillance can help by filtering activity and identifying events that match predefined criteria.
It would be relatively ineffective if this system sent an alert every time someone walks past a camera. But instead, for example, a system could flag movement inside a restricted area after hours. Or licence plate recognition could help monitor vehicles entering or leaving particular areas. Smart security systems can also make investigations easier. Instead of searching through hours of footage manually, security personnel may be able to narrow recordings by time, location, vehicle or type of activity.
But Smarter Doesn’t Always Mean Better
Understandably, there can be a temptation to assume that more technology automatically means more security. But smart systems introduce additional points of failure. They can depend on power, connectivity, software and correct configuration. Poorly calibrated systems can also generate false alerts, eventually causing staff to ignore notifications altogether.
Then there’s complexity. A system might have an impressive list of capabilities, but those capabilities don’t mean much if employees don’t understand how to use them or nobody responds when an alert comes through. The right technology needs to be selected against the actual risks of a property. Where a small business with one entrance may not need an elaborate AI video surveillance network, a large construction site would benefit significantly from intelligent monitoring because of the sheer volume of activity taking place across the property.
Putting the Two Together: 1 + 1 = 3
The very best security strategies tend to combine smart and simple measures. They both become greater than the sum of their parts when integrated. Start with the fundamentals. Secure doors, windows, gates and perimeter areas. Make entrances visible and eliminate poorly lit spaces. Use signage and visible surveillance to create a clear deterrent.
Then add smart technology where it provides a genuine advantage. Intelligent cameras can monitor areas that are difficult to supervise manually. Access control can restrict sensitive spaces while creating an audit trail, and automated alerts can help security teams identify and respond to unusual activity quickly.
Finally, connect technology with people. Security personnel can investigate alerts, conduct patrols and respond to situations that technology alone cannot resolve. In this model, smart surveillance becomes an extra set of eyes rather than a replacement for human judgement.
Key Takeaways
The future of security is likely to borrow from tech innovations while keeping firmly in the lane of traditional, physical measures. Dumb security measures provide a first layer of protection. Smart technology makes detection and surveillance more efficient. Human security professionals can then provide context, judgement and physical intervention when required.
The goal is to build a security system that suits the property, discourages unwanted behaviour, identifies genuine threats and provides a reliable response when something goes wrong. And, most often, the smartest security strategy is knowing when to use both dumb and smart features.

articles.title: Party’s Over for Crypto Scammers Who Went on a Spending Spree After a $240 Million Bitcoin Theft
articles.text:
They pulled off one of the largest cryptocurrency thefts in U.S. history, duping a stranger out of bitcoin worth over $240 million. They tried to hide their digital fingerprints, carrying out a sophisticated scheme to launder the proceeds.
And then the party started.
The scammers — a network of young men in their late teens or early 20s — celebrated the August 2024 heist by embarking on a wild spending spree. They purchased fleets of sports cars, flew on private jets, hired security guards and rented mansions in Miami and the Hamptons. An alleged ringleader, 22-year-old Malone Lam, spent over $569,000 in one evening at a Los Angeles night club.
Their bender lasted a month before FBI agents arrested Lam on charges that he organized a “social engineering” attack on the Washington, D.C., resident. Lam, an eighth-grade dropout from Singapore, has a plea agreement hearing set for Tuesday. His conviction would be a capstone for the government’s investigation.
The charges against Lam and 17 others are an extreme example of an increasingly common form of cybercrime. Complaints of cryptocurrency investment fraud to the FBI rose by nearly 50% in 2025, while Republican President Donald Trump’s administration largely abandoned a regulatory crackdown on the volatile industry.
Last year, the Justice Department disbanded a unit dedicated to prosecuting crypto-related crimes. Meanwhile, crypto companies that complained of unfair treatment during Democratic President Joe Biden’s presidency are enjoying the government’s hands-off approach under Trump, who took in roughly $1.2 billion from his crypto businesses in 2025.
Cybersecurity researcher Allison Nixon, who has spent years tracking The Com, an underground subculture of young hackers united by the “insane amount of money” that crypto fraud can generate, advocates for more law enforcement resources to go after them.
“If we don’t seriously ramp up the resources to take these people down and do it faster, then it’s going to spread more and more,” she said.
Scammers nabbed millions though ‘social engineering’ heist
A man identified as “Victim 7” in court filings was at home in Washington on Aug. 18, 2024, when his phone rang. The first caller identified himself as a Google representative inquiring about attempts to breach his account. A second, claiming to be from the Gemini crypto exchange, warned the man of a malware attack affecting his crypto wallet.
The callers manipulated the man into giving them access to his Google Drive and revealing security codes that allowed Lam to siphon off over 4,100 bitcoin, according to prosecutors. They said Lam and his friends on the calls — Veer Chetal and Jeandiel Serrano — targeted the man because he was a wealthy, longtime crypto investor.
A private recording captured the moment when the friends realized how much money they just stole, according to a video posted by a well-known private investigator of cryptocurrency crimes who goes by ZachXBT.
“Oh, my God! Bro, bro, I’m going to spaz out!” a voice on the video said.
Once they swiped the man’s savings, they used money laundering specialists to wash it through multiple exchange platforms and convert virtual currency into government-issued cash.
It wasn’t the first social engineering scam for the friends, who met in online gaming forums. They had teamed up on other multimillion-dollar thefts since late 2023 using a similar playbook, according to prosecutors.
This time, however, one of them made a costly mistake: Serrano failed to conceal his IP address when he created an account on a cryptocurrency exchange to hold nearly $30 million in stolen crypto, according to prosecutors. Investigators linked the IP address to a home in Encino, California, that Serrano was renting for $47,500 a month.
Lavish spending quickly drew attention
Serrano was vacationing in the Maldives when investigators identified him as a suspect. Lam was in Los Angeles, where he and friends spent $4 million at nightclubs in one month, authorities say. Chetal gifted a Lamborghini to his parents and hid a duffel bag filled with $500,000 in cash in their laundry machine.
Word of their windfall quickly spread in crypto scammers’ circles. A week after the big score, Chetal’s parents were driving in Danbury, Connecticut, when several masked men cut them off, forced them out of their new car, beat Chetal’s father with a baseball bat, shoved the couple into a van and bound their hands.
The captors, from Miami, had intended to use Chetal’s parents as leverage for extorting him into giving up his share of the stolen crypto. But the ransom plot fell apart when witnesses notified police, who apprehended the carjackers.
The FBI showed up to search Chetal’s apartment in Brunswick, New Jersey, on Sept. 9, 2024, and found $37 million in stolen crypto in his possession. He agreed to cooperate with their investigation.
Lam was attracting attention, too, for spending hundreds of thousands of dollars a night at clubs and tossing handbags worth tens of thousands of dollars to women in the crowds. He also used stolen cryptocurrency to buy a $2 million watch and over 30 cars, including custom Porsches, Lamborghinis and Ferraris, according to the FBI.
“This luxury lifestyle, of which so many young men and women could only dream, was just built on a foundation of fraud,” a prosecutor, William Hart, said during a recent sentencing hearing for a money laundering co-defendant.
‘Ferris Bueller gone bad’
Serrano was wearing a $500,000 watch when FBI agents arrested him at Los Angeles International Airport on Sept. 18, 2024. He initially professed his innocence but soon admitted to having roughly $20 million of the D.C. man’s stolen crypto, prosecutors said.
Lam was arrested at one of his Miami mansions on the same day as Serrano. An off-duty law enforcement officer had tipped off Lam that authorities were on their way to arrest him, the indictment says.
“We always talked about what it would be like if I were to go down, but never thought it would be this crazy,” Lam told associates from jail on a recorded call, according to his indictment.
The judge for Lam’s initial court appearance in Miami sounded astonished by a prosecutor’s summary of his lavish spending.
“I could only think of Ferris Bueller gone bad,” U.S. Magistrate Alicia Valle said, referring to the school-skipping protagonist of the 1986 movie “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.”
Lam’s capture didn’t stop the splurging. Ferro, who pleaded guilty to a racketeering conspiracy charge last year, used stolen funds to cover Lam’s legal expenses.
Judgment Days
Eighteen defendants have been charged. Lam would be the 11th to plead guilty. At Lam’s first court appearance, a prosecutor estimated that his sentencing guidelines would recommend a prison term of at least 14 years upon conviction.
U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly, who presides over Lam’s case, already has sentenced three of his co-conspirators. She sentenced two money launderers to prison terms of approximately six years.
Chetal pleaded guilty to conspiracy charges in November 2024 and awaits sentencing. Serrano’s charges remain pending.
Tucker Desmond, who pleaded guilty to destroying evidence of other plotters’ crimes, was sentenced to probation. Desmond apologized at his sentencing hearing in March, saying he “got obsessed with the image of success rather than actually becoming a hard-working individual myself.”
Ferro declined to address the court during his sentencing hearing in May. His attorney, Kevin Wilson, described the co-defendants as mischievous “young kids,” but the judge didn’t accept that as an excuse.
“Being young only goes so far,” Kollar-Kotelly said.
Related: Seizing Cryptocurrency: How is Law Enforcement Tracing and Recovering Bitcoin Payments?

articles.title: España quiere dejar de depender de Huawei. El problema es que primero tiene que pagar millones por seguir dependiendo de Huawei
articles.text:
España quiere reducir la dependencia de Huawei en una de sus principales redes públicas, pero no puede hacerlo de buenas a primeras. Red.es acaba de poner en marcha dos contratos por un total de 10,3 millones de euros que garantizan durante 38 y 40 meses tanto las operaciones como el mantenimiento de la infraestructura actual de RedIRIS. En esos contratos incluso se exigen conocimientos y certificaciones sobre tecnología de Huawei, y eso demuestra que para poder abandonar a la empresa china, España ha comprado justo lo que necesitaba: tiempo.
Una dependencia que viene de lejos. RedIRIS es la gran red académica y científica española. Cuenta con más de 16.000 km de fibra, conecta más de 500 instituciones y da servicio a cerca de cinco millones de usuarios. Incluso transporta datos de determinados servicios del Ministerio de Defensa. En 2020, Telefónica recibió un contrato de 5,5 millones de euros para sustituir la anterior infraestructura de Alcatel por equipos de Huawei y así elevar la velocidad de 10 a 100 Gbps en esas transferencias. El problema es que desde entonces la dependencia de esos equipos de Huawei es notable.
Lo más barato era seguir con Huawei. En julio Red.es anunció su intención de dar un nuevo salto de 100 a 400 Gbps, y en 2025 preparó un contrato de 9,8 millones con Telefónica. En la documentación se dejaba claro que los nuevos componentes debían instalarse en los routers de Huawei que ya estaban funcionando. No había que rediseñar la red, y bastaba con ampliar lo existente. El célebre "vendor lock-in" entraba en acción: una vez que creas algo alrededor de un proveedor, seguir con él suele convertirse en la opción más cómoda.
Entonces llegó la geopolítica. El contrato fue cancelado en agosto de 2025 después de la polémica de utilizar tecnología china en una infraestructura sensible. El Ministerio para la Transformación Digital habló en aquel momento de un cambio de "estrategia digital y autonomía tecnológica". La decisión no equivalía al veto total de Huawei —España no dispone de una "entity list" como EEUU—, pero sí suponía renunciar a la solución técnica más asequible y sencilla: seguir con los equipos que ya estaban instalados.
Deshacerse de Huawei lleva tiempo. Red.es adjudicó en julio a Telefónica un contrato de 4,29 millones de euros y 38 meses para mantener la electrónica de las capas 2 y 3 de esta infraestructura. El 6 de agosto aprobó otro, presupuestado en seis millones y de 40 meses, para la monitorización, operación y soporte avanzado. En este último es donde se valora que los ingenieros implicados en el proyecto dispongan de certificación HCIP de Huawei. Ese dinero, insistimos, se paga para comprar tiempo que permita trabajar en la sustitución de esos equipos.
De momento no hay alternativa. Red.es abrió el 15 de julio una consulta preliminar al mercado para estudiar cómo renovar completamente la infraestructura y poder incorporar interfaces de hasta 400 Gbps. Las empresas interesadas tienen hasta el 30 de octubre de 2026 para presentar sus propuestas. Después tendrán que evaluarse esas propuestas y entrará en acción toda la maquinaria burocrática (pliegos, licitaciones, adjudicaciones) y la ejecución de ese proyecto. Es todo un desafío: hay que migrar el tráfico de la infraestructura actual sin interrumpir el servicio que utilizan universidades, supercomputadores y centros de investigación.
Del bloqueo software al hardware. Normalmente solemos asociar el vendor lock-in a enormes plataformas software de Oracle, Microsoft o AWS, pero una red de comunicaciones como la que hay ahora que reemplazar añade esa dimensión "tangible" del cambio. Cambiar de proveedor puede significar sustituir equipos que aún funcionan y mantener durante cierto tiempo ambas infraestructuras corriendo en paralelo para tener un plan B.
Un aviso para la ambiciosa soberanía europea. Lo que está pasando con Red.es sirve como precedente para tener claro que esa independencia y soberanía tecnológica que busca Europa es prácticamente imposible de conseguir. Es factible sustuir algunos procesos y componentes software e incluso hardware, pero ni mucho menos todos ellos. Pero es que además hacerlo lleva tiempo y dinero, porque mientras se sustituyen esos equipos o plataformas, hay que seguir pagando para que los ya instalados sigan funcionando.

articles.title: An AI-developed drug appeared to make patients biologically younger in a clinical trial
articles.text:
What just happened? As we all know, we're still waiting for the cancer cure people said AI would bring. However, an AI-generated drug has shown signs of a different breakthrough: slowing the aging process. There's a catch, naturally: changes in aging markers don't prove we'll soon be living to 150.
The experimental drug, rentosertib, comes from Insilico Medicine and was developed to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a disease that progressively scars the lungs.
According to the company, AI helped identify its target, a protein called TNIK, and design the molecule that inhibits it.
Now, a study published September 7 in Nature Biotechnology has revisited data from a phase 2a trial involving 71 patients in China. The aging analysis covered 42 participants, with an average age of about 67, whose blood samples were tracked over 12 weeks.
Researchers applied six aging clocks – computational models that use blood proteins to estimate biological age or mortality risk. All six detected shifts toward younger predicted ages among treated patients, while placebo recipients showed little change or slight increases.
The results weren't identical across doses or measurements. At week four, patients taking 60mg daily showed reductions of roughly 2.7 to 3.5 years on four chronological-age clocks. The two mortality-based clocks didn't show significant changes. Taking 30mg twice daily produced the most consistent signal overall.
Before anyone starts planning an extra century of retirement, those figures describe model predictions. The researchers acknowledge that they can't fully separate effects on aging from improvements in lung disease. Establishing whether the drug benefits people without that condition will require further research.
It was reported last year that scientists had developed blood tests that estimate how quickly individual organs are aging. Such tools could help identify disease risks, but younger-looking test results still need to translate into meaningful health benefits.
Insilico has already announced a phase 3 trial targeting lung disease, expected to enroll 320 participants and measure changes in lung function over 52 weeks. The company says rentosertib remains investigational and has not received regulatory approval.
The findings also arrive amid some AI-based longevity optimism. Futurist Peter Diamandis previously predicted that the key to living longer is to make it into the 2030s, then let AI take it from there.
There's also Bryan Johnson, the man whose quest to live forever was turned into a Netflix documentary. He'll likely be paying close attention to reports on rentosertib, having long talked about how AI-developed drugs will increase human lifespans.

articles.title: A word with a woman who’s trying to pull off a crossbody phone strap
articles.text:
Oh, this thing? It’s just a crossbody strap. It’s a fun and youthful way to carry your phone. It’s all the rage with Europeans and young people. I love it, and I definitely don’t feel weird and self-conscious using it. Plus, it’s great to have a $700 investment dangling near your waist while you walk down the street. Kind of a thrill.
A word with a woman who’s trying to pull off a crossbody phone strap
She’s beauty and she’s grace, she’s got embarrassment written all over her face.
Stylish? Yeah, I guess it looks pretty cool. Especially when I pair it with an oversized jacket and it kind of bunches the fabric up around my armpit. It’s a pretty seamless addition to my wardrobe since I basically live in Tevas and a pair of athleisure leggings from Target. I am a Target Circle member, in fact. I don’t like to brag about it, but that’s how plugged in I am to the latest fashion trends. Anyway, one of my friends watched me sling the crossbody over my shoulder and said, “I feel like I’m hanging out with Rick Steves.”
Convenient? Totally. It’s so easy to grab my phone, wrestle it around so the screen is facing me, and bang out a text without missing a beat. Way easier than just grabbing it out of my jacket pocket. Plus, I always have my phone handy for tap-to-pay. Sometimes I have to lean in and do a mini squat to reach the pay terminal, but that’s a little bonus workout. That’s just the kind of thing you can do when you live a soft pants lifestyle.
One of my friends watched me sling the crossbody over my shoulder and said, ‘I feel like I’m hanging out with Rick Steves’
You know what else? It’s too goddamn dark in bars these days, or they’re making the print smaller on the menus. Maybe both. But that’s not a problem when you have your phone on a crossbody strap. Just hit that flashlight toggle (on purpose, for a change) and you’ve got a handy reading light at your side. Nothing complements the ambiance of a moody cocktail lounge like 50 lumens of bright white LEDs aimed at your receipt while you figure out whether or not a service charge was included.
Honestly? It would be useful if the crossbody could hold other stuff, too. Like maybe my keys, some tissues, and a little notebook. Loose change, Carmex, that kind of thing. And maybe I can take my phone out of it when I get home, hang it up on the coat rack, and have it ready to go for my next outing. A crossbody, but a little bigger so it can hold all the stuff you leave the house with. I bet you they sell one at Target.

articles.title: Arm debuts next-gen semi-custom Neoverse CSS N4 ‘Ranger’ platform — compute subsystem packs up to 128 cores per die on TSMC N3P
articles.text:
Arm debuts next-gen semi-custom Neoverse CSS N4 ‘Ranger’ platform — compute subsystem packs up to 128 cores per die on TSMC N3P
Putting a little pep in Neoverse N-series’ step.
Arm is bringing its next-gen Neoverse CSS N4 platforms to the cloud, sporting up to 128 cores per die, built on TSMC’s N3P process. Arm’s Compute Subsystem, or CSS, is a semi-custom program that allows customers to design a chip based on Arm’s IP, configuring components like core count, cache size, I/O, and connectivity to fit their specific needs. It’s the same platform we’ve seen at work everywhere from CPUs at Azure and Google Cloud to DPUs at Nvidia and Intel.
Arm says Neoverse CSS N4 supports between eight and 128 Neoverse N4 cores, running up to 3.8 GHz. Presumably, the clocks drop as the core count rises; Arm didn’t clarify the maximum clocks for each possible configuration. At a system level, Neoverse CSS N4 can scale beyond 128 cores, with support for multi-chiplet and multi-socket designs, and with support for UCIe through chip-to-chip interconnects, as well as “partner-specific PNYs.”
The platform supports either DDR5 or LPDDR6, and features up to 256 MB of L3 cache per die. For local cache, Arm includes up to 2 MB of L2 per core, as well as 64 KB of L1 instruction cache and 64 KB of L1 data cache per core. For I/O, Arm supports up to 128 lanes of PCIe 7/6 and CXL 4.0.
It’s a significant upgrade over the Neoverse CSS N2 platform, which topped out at just 64 cores, 1 MB of L2 cache per core, and 64 MB of L3 cache, paired with either DDR5 or LPDDR5 and 64 PCIe 5.0/CXL lanes.
With 128 cores running at 3GHz and 2MB of L2 cache per core, Arm says Neoverse CSS N4 delivers twice the socket performance of Neoverse N3, 1.25x performance per watt, and 1.75x the memory bandwidth.
Arm’s N-series cores are optimized for performance per watt, while its V-series cores are targeting maximum performance. For instance, Arm used the Neoverse CSS V3 building blocks for its own AGI CPU, and Nvidia used Neoverse V2 for its last-gen Grace CPU (the Vera CPU uses a custom core). AWS has also used Neoverse V-series cores for its own Graviton chips, as does Google Cloud for Axion.
N-series cores aren’t usually deployed in high-performance CPUs. Rather, they fit into less-performant accelerators, such as Intel’s IPU Adapter E2100, which is built on Neoverse N1 cores. We’ve also seen it deployed in less-demanding, cloud-based workloads, such as through Microsoft’s Azure Cobalt 100, which is built on Neoverse N2. Cobalt 200 moved onto Neoverse V3.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
We don’t know much about the Neoverse N4 cores, codenamed Dionysus. Arm’s 2024 roadmap indicated we’ll see Arm Neoverse CSS V4, as well, codenamed Vega.
Unlike a traditional announcement from Intel, AMD, or the various partners that build on Arm, we won’t see Neoverse N4 cores in the wild for a while. The announcement Arm is making is for those who are building on the CSS platform, leveraging Arm’s validated building blocks to create semi-custom silicon quickly. Arm has yet to announce any partners, though traditionally, only a few large CSS contracts are needed.
Additional Arm AGI CPU deployments
Alongside the announcement of Arm Neoverse CSS N4, the company revealed additional deployments of its own AGI chip, which is built with Neoverse V3 cores. The company revealed that Oracle and ByteDance will deploy AGI chips, alongside previously announced deployments at Meta, Lenovo, SAP, OpenAI, Cloudflare, and others.
Although Arm has talked a lot about AGI, including a deep dive into the chip’s architecture at Hot Chips, we’ve yet to see real-world performance numbers. That’s not uncommon, especially among more recent Arm-based chips. For instance, we only have gen-on-gen comparisons for Microsoft’s Azure Cobalt 200 and AWS’ Graviton5. Arm has vaguely referenced performance by saying AGI offers “more than 2x the performance per rack compared to the latest x86 systems,” though those claims are based on internal estimates, not real benchmarks.
AGI is a dual-die CPU with up to 136 Neoverse V3 cores and up to 272 MB of L3 cache that can clock up to 3.7 GHz. It has the specs to match any high-end x86 design currently on the market, built on a 3nm node and packing up to 6TB of memory capacity per chip, running at up to DDR5-8800. Perhaps the biggest difference compared to AMD and Intel was Arm’s decision to include the memory and I/O on the same die as compute, which it says leads to sub-100ns memory latency.
It’s Arm’s first attempt at its own production silicon, though it’s also been positioned so far as a vehicle for the broader applications of Arm in the data center. Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta, Google Cloud, and others build custom chips based on Arm IP, which still seems to be the primary goal, even with AGI in the mix.
